page_placements.theme: Weight edits can remove refusal incompletely (single rank-1 passes, skipped residual writers, low-bit edits)

record.file_problem: README and repository file list only; code was not read or run.
record.tranche_reason: The README reports refusal-score outcomes after weight orthogonalization based on activation-derived refusal directions, a different intervention from activation projection.
record.gate_note: The README reports two aggregate refusal-score reductions. It gives no per-prompt or per-run results. Method or configuration details mentioned without outcomes are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The README reports refusal-score outcomes on Gemma-2B-IT after weight orthogonalization along a harmful-minus-harmless activation direction. That is the abliteration edit (V2), which is equivalent to directional ablation (V1). The refusal score appears to be token- or phrase-based and its definition is not given, so the measure may differ from the original's. The evidence is a single approximate 'typical' figure with no baseline, sample size or uncertainty.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The README says weight orthogonalization typically gives ~6% lower refusal scores on harmful prompts and ~43% lower on harmless prompts. It also asserts, without reported numbers, that the method keeps the model helpful and safe.
record.recipe_differences: The README describes computing refusal directions from activation differences and orthogonalizing model weights, rather than projecting the direction out of activations at every layer and position or adding it. This is a tool repository; code was not read or run.

fits_no_version.finding: Abliteration reduced refusal scores much more on harmless prompts (~43%) than on harmful prompts (~6%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight orthogonalization along the refusal direction can mainly lower refusal-related scores on harmless prompts, affecting over-refusal more than harmful-request refusal.

record.problems: The README gives only approximate aggregate reductions, without baselines, sample sizes, uncertainty, controls, or reported results for retained capabilities. Code and results were not independently inspected or run.
record.rows_left_out: No reported outcome rows were left out.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; retention of other abilities (no capability results despite the README's claim of maintained helpfulness); activation-level ablation.
Released models beyond Gemma-2B-IT; capability cost of the edit; how the saved checkpoint behaves under generation-based refusal judging.

record.verdict_notes: This is a hobby GitHub repository with no paper and only README-level results. The figures are described as 'typical' approximations, with no baselines, sample sizes, uncertainty or definition of the refusal score. The config mentions positive/negative token sets, suggesting a logit-based score. A saved checkpoint exists, but no results are reported for it. Give this study very low weight.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report activation ablation at every layer and position, adding the direction, or whether other abilities remain intact.
Does not report complete removal of refusal or separate results for released checkpoints; the README reports score reductions.

tranche.reason: The edit is the same as the original weight edit (weight orthogonalization along a harmful-minus-harmless direction), but the measure differs. It is an undefined token- and phrase-based 'refusal score', not the original's substring and Llama Guard scores, so T1 doesn't apply. Gemma-2B-IT isn't a new setting, so T3 doesn't either. The record's 'different' reasoning mentions the method, but the real difference is the measure.

source_check.notes: The pack listed its verdicts without [lN] ids, so I assigned l1 (V2) and l2 (V1) by their order in the pack. The study is a README with no data or logs. Its 'refusal score' uses positive and negative token sets plus refusal phrases from src/config.py, which isn't in the text. The harmless-prompt drop (43%) is larger than the harmful one (6%), which suggests the score isn't a refusal rate. Treat both figures as anecdotal.

statements.correction: README: orthogonalization 'typically achieves' ~6% reduction in refusal scores on harmful prompts (Gemma-2B-IT experiment). No baseline, n or score definition. Relative vs absolute not stated. The author presents this as success. The record's verdicts for V1 and V2 are limits_scope, not challenges.
statements.problem: The ~6% figure is right, but listing this study under a 'challenges' label conflicts with its own verdict (limits_scope). A ~6% reduction is a small move in the right direction, not an absent effect. 'Keeps much of its refusal' can't be shown when the baseline and metric are unknown and it is unclear whether the 6% is relative or absolute.
